title: Judgment and the Survey Decision
prework: Watch the Module 1 videos, including the short geometric-model bridge. Read the Module 1 note and bring a public company decision for your individual Discussion 1.
output: An individual Discussion 1 draft and a candidate decision to discuss with your project team.

slides.title: Judgment and the Survey Decision
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M1S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Question Order in a Published Survey
lines: What changed before the country question?
slides.notes: Pew reports 78% dissatisfied when the country question came first and 88% when presidential approval immediately preceded it. These are published percentages of U.S. adults, not a new estimate. The page does not supply arm sizes here, so no confidence interval is inferred. Ask students to explain the stable-answer assumption and then name a possible contextual process. The pattern alone does not identify a quantum mechanism. Carry one assumption into Discussion 1.

chart.caption: Pew Research Center, December 2008 U.S. poll.

slides.title: The Same Destination, Different Experiences
lines: Which experience comes first may affect the later choice.
slides.notes: The two illustrated paths reach the same pavilion after encountering a market and a garden in different orders. Treat this as an analogy for sequence, not evidence about human behavior. Translate it into two survey procedures.

slides.title: A Fictional Service Launch
lines: A company must choose how to introduce a data-enabled service.
One survey leads with convenience; another leads with privacy.
The focal outcome is support for launch.
slides.notes: This is a fictional planning case with no reported results. Hold facts fixed. Ask what the manager wants to decide and which customer outcome would be useful. Define data-enabled service in the discussion as a service that uses customer information to provide a benefit.

slides.title: A Fair Comparison in the Survey Tool
lines: The order of A and B varies. F stays last.
Which setting preserves the final decision?
slides.notes: The screenshot is a documented product example, not this course survey. Have students draft the same convenience question A and privacy question B for both ABF and BAF. The launch-support question F stays last. Hold facts, response options, and respondent population fixed. Advanced randomization can preserve positions; do not assume randomizing every question implements ABF versus BAF. Explain how order will be assigned and recorded. Save the wording for the proposal.

image.alt: Official Qualtrics dialog shows no randomization, all-question randomization, a subset option, and advanced randomization. The advanced option is highlighted in the source.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: question randomization.

slides.title: A Fixed-Rate Benchmark
lines: Two assessed action rates are 0.30 and 0.70.
Can any weighted average reach 0.80?
State the assumption that this comparison tests.
slides.notes: Use the displayed line or the Module 3 notebook mixture helper. The values are imposed illustrations, not survey findings. A weighted average cannot exceed both fixed inputs. Applying this benchmark to another procedure requires carrying the conditional rates across procedures. Consider how a process-dependent alternative could change them.

chart.caption: Imposed conditional rates: 0.30 and 0.70; weights range from 0 to 1.

slides.title: A Test of the Alternative
lines: Could attention, memory, or learning explain the difference?
What does that explanation predict?
Which new comparison would distinguish it?
slides.notes: Each group names one specific alternative and an observable implication. A classical process can depend on context. Avoid using classical as a synonym for an unchanging answer. Connect the discussion to the strongest-rival requirement in Project Part 1.

slides.title: Predictions for a New Procedure
lines: Which new observation would separate the models?
slides.notes: The first two values are imposed earlier results that both models reproduce. The final values are competing predictions, not observations. A new procedure is held out when its results are kept separate during fitting and model selection. Ask students to name assumptions that justify their predictions, then write one comparison for their own proposal. These anonymous models illustrate prediction; neither is designated quantum or classical.

chart.caption: Imposed predictions. Both models match the earlier results.

slides.title: The Discussion Argument
lines: Name the company decision and public evidence.
Explain the response procedure and its hidden assumption.
Propose one informative comparison.
slides.notes: Draft an outline for M1A1 using your own company. Peer discussion can improve the reasoning; submit your own post and response under the assessment instructions. Use the public evidence to ground the frames rather than treating the fictional service case as a documented company.

slides.title: The Next Workshop Step
lines: Retain the draft argument and question wording.
Identify one source or design issue to resolve.
Bring the decision statement to Project Studio 1.
slides.notes: Exit note: identify the benchmark, its assumption, and your next evidence-gathering step. This is workshop progress, not a new graded submission.

output: A shared company decision, research question, candidate frames, and initial entries in the team’s AI Attribution and contribution logs.

lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming

M1S2
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Inputs to a Recommendation
lines: A parent may play music for a child.
Should every play shape future recommendations?
slides.notes: Spotify introduced playlist exclusion in February 2023. Use the displayed nursery-rhyme example to distinguish an observed play from the listener’s preference for future recommendations. The product feature is documented; its effect on satisfaction is a hypothesis to test. Ask students to name a product owner, feasible actions, and an outcome for their own company. Avoid claiming that this interface demonstrates quantum cognition.

image.alt: Spotify’s official nursery-rhyme playlist menu includes Exclude from your taste profile. The source highlights that control.

slides.caption: Spotify launch example, February 2023.

slides.title: Evidence and the Proposed Test
lines: Which claim in your proposal still needs evidence?
slides.notes: The first two entries follow from Spotify’s public example. The audit entry describes a proposed study, not an observed company result. Students add two public sources for their chosen company, recording source, date, and exact supported claim. Keep a company announcement distinct from evidence of causal effectiveness.
slides.caption: Worked source ledger for the Spotify example.

slides.title: Two Competing Considerations
lines: Explain why both considerations matter here.
Write a neutral question for each.
Keep the focal decision separate.
slides.notes: Work on A, B, and F. Ask whether each consideration follows from the institutional setting. Define unfamiliar terms in the question itself. Avoid telling a synthetic respondent how the experiment is expected to turn out.

slides.title: A Research Question You Can Answer
lines: Name the response procedure.
Name the focal outcome and comparison.
State the scope of the model-panel evidence.
slides.notes: A usable question might ask whether the tested model gives different launch-support rates after two specified frame orders. Separate that question from whether real customers support launch. Draft the proposal research question.

slides.title: Volume for a Complete Audit
lines: What volume can you collect and document?
slides.notes: A record here is one completed condition for one persona and repetition. Required records equal personas × six conditions × repetitions. This is accounting, not a precision guarantee, and records need not equal API calls or token costs. Check access, time, approved spending, and the number of calls within each conversation. A pilot tests the workflow. Use the collection guide and record the scope feedback before project collection.

chart.caption: Six conditions per persona. Counts exclude retries and pilot work.

slides.title: Peer Review of the Proposal
lines: Can a reader identify the management decision?
Do the frames follow from the public evidence?
Is the strongest alternative specific and testable?
slides.notes: Exchange outlines with another team. Give one substantive suggestion tied to the proposal rubric. Each team discusses the feedback, agrees on revisions, and records who will make and check each change.

slides.title: Your Judgment and AI Use
lines: Each member records an initial judgment before AI use.
Log who used the tool and who checked the result.
Agree on the team’s revision and its reason.
slides.notes: Project Part 1 is AIAS 3. Follow the assessment instructions and keep the AI Attribution Log. The log should document judgment, not merely list a tool name.

slides.title: The Proposal Draft
lines: Save one team decision and three draft questions.
Assign tasks and a reviewer for each substantive step.
Record the design choices still open for Module 2.
slides.notes: This checkpoint prepares the proposal due at the end of Week 3. Consult Canvas for the exact date. It is not an additional graded deliverable.

title: Interpreting Order Effects
prework: Watch the Module 2 videos, including intervals and tolerances. Run the order-and-QQ notebook and bring your team’s preliminary A/B/F battery.
output: An individual Discussion 2 outline and proposed thresholds and rival tests to review with your project team.

slides.title: Interpreting Order Effects
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M2S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Order Differences and QQ
lines: Which statistic compares F across orders?
Which statistic compares A/B agreement?
What records does each require?
slides.notes: Give students two minutes to write their answers. The focal difference uses F yes rates; q uses actual paired A/B responses within each order. Clarify only the distinctions that remain uncertain.

slides.title: An Imposed Answer-Pair Table
lines: Both columns contain 100 illustrative interviews.
slides.notes: The table consistently uses A rows and B columns, including for BA. These are imposed counts and not human observations. Students should verify totals before computing rates.

slides.title: Agreement and the A-Yes Rate
lines: Why can agreement stay fixed while an answer rate changes?
slides.notes: A-yes is (30+10)/100=.40 in AB and (45+25)/100=.70 in BA. Agreement is (30+40)/100=.70 in AB and (45+25)/100=.70 in BA, so q=.00 for the agreement-difference definition. A-yes is a marginal answer rate, not F. This table contains no F responses; it cannot establish a focal decision effect. Ask students which records their proposal needs for each statistic.

chart.yTitle: Share of 100 interviews in each order
chart.caption: Calculated from the imposed answer-pair table on the previous slide.

slides.title: A Classical Sequential Explanation
lines: Inspect the transition rules in the notebook.
The rules vary with which question comes first.
Which extra prediction would test this explanation?
slides.notes: Run classical_order_example. In AB, A yes is .4 and B yes conditional on A is .75 or 1/3. In BA, B yes is .5 and A yes conditional on B is .9 or .5. Ordinary probabilities generate the table with q=0. Source: the course’s constructed example; Dzhafarov and Kon, https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.07847.

slides.title: Intervals Against a Practical Range
lines: Use a prespecified tolerance of ±5 percentage points.
slides.notes: The intervals are illustrative inputs, not estimates from a dataset. Ask students to classify each and justify the action. A and C lie inside the practical range; B is unresolved. Revise the table if the class chooses a different managerial tolerance.

slides.title: Resampling Complete Personas
lines: Which six records travel together when a persona is drawn?
slides.notes: Each of three personas has one record in each of six conditions. One bootstrap draw selects persona 02 twice, persona 03 once, and persona 01 zero times. Copy all six records each time a persona is selected. This example explains the resampling unit; three personas are not an adequate sample-size recommendation. For the course audit, retain the complete persona blocks and all repetitions in each selected block. For independently assigned human respondents, the resampling design would follow the actual human sampling structure.

chart.caption: Toy example: draw personas 02, 02, 03 from three complete blocks.

slides.title: Design Revisions
lines: Freeze A, B, F, coding, and collection conditions.
Choose a practical threshold and q tolerance.
Write a fair test of the strongest alternative.
slides.notes: Students revise their own proposal. Thresholds should follow the managerial decision and feasible precision. The teaching value of .05 is not a universal threshold. Save the rationale in the proposal and log any later changes.

slides.title: The Interpretation Paragraph
lines: Explain why order and QQ answer different questions.
Describe what an uncertain interval leaves unresolved.
Use that reasoning in Discussion 2.
slides.notes: Write your own M2A1 discussion outline. Then identify one proposal weakness to discuss with your team. Discussion 2 is individual; the proposal is a shared team submission.

title: Battery Design and Proposal Workshop
prework: Watch Module 2 first. Bring the team’s working proposal, question battery, evidence ledger, and collection guide. The proposal is due at the end of Week 3; this meeting develops the draft.
output: A revised team proposal draft and a list of issues to resolve before the end-of-Week-3 submission.

slides.title: Battery Design and Proposal Workshop
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M2S2 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes: Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

slides.title: A Battery for the Service Decision
lines: How would you revise these questions for your company?
slides.notes: A battery is a set of questions used together. These shortened prompts illustrate structure; students must specify the service, features, privacy practices, and neutral wording. In the constructed ABF and BAF arms, keep F last and retain actual prior answers. Follow the collection guide for all six conditions. Define any specialized terms in the survey itself.
slides.caption: Fictional planning example. Supply the same service facts in every arm.

slides.title: Six Conditions, One Persona Grid
slides.notes: The isolated conditions ask every question in a fresh conversation. Constructed conditions retain actual prior answers. Direct and assessed arms supply the separate procedural comparison. An ordinary all-at-once panel is optional and does not replace a required arm.
table: A, B, F / B, A, F
A → B → F / B → A → F

slides.title: The Final Question Has a Fixed Position
lines: Randomizing questions and selecting a subset change different things.
Which items vary, and which position stays fixed?
slides.notes: Use this product example to inspect a design choice before collecting data. The screenshot shows a general control, not a configured ABF/BAF study. Students identify how their implementation preserves F last while varying A and B. Hold the fact sheet, coding, and intended context fixed. Pilot both orders and save the exact prompts, actual answers, and conversation history.

image.alt: The upper portion of the official advanced-randomization dialog contrasts fixed display order with randomize questions. The displayed example text belongs to Qualtrics, not the course battery.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: advanced randomization.

slides.title: The Record of What Each Person Saw
lines: The assigned order and the observed order should agree.
Can your records reconstruct the question sequence?
slides.notes: Qualtrics documents an option to export viewing order. The course model-panel workflow needs the analogous evidence: condition, persona, repetition, actual prompt order, response, and conversation history. Set the collection volume, model version, settings, and stopping rule before collection. Students save a pilot record and verify it can reproduce a response path. This slide does not require students to use Qualtrics.

image.alt: An official Qualtrics export dialog has the option Export viewing order data for randomized surveys checked and outlined.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: viewing-order export.

slides.title: Precision and the Collection Plan
lines: How does this uncertainty compare with your practical threshold?
slides.notes: The displayed normal-approximation half-width for a difference is 1.96 × sqrt(0.25/n+0.25/n) ×100 percentage points, where n is observations per independent arm. Values are about 19.6, 13.9, 9.8, 6.9, and 4.9 points. This conservative planning illustration is not the audit’s paired-persona bootstrap interval or a sample-size prescription. Dependence, rare subgroups, and invalid answers affect precision. Students freeze their substantive thresholds and appropriate analysis before observing the project results.

chart.xTitle: Observations per arm (each step doubles n)
chart.caption: Planning illustration: two independent arms, each with yes probability 0.50.

slides.title: Peer Review Against the Rubric
lines: Find one claim without enough evidence.
Find one design choice that could change the result.
Propose a concrete revision.
slides.notes: Partners use the proposal rubric. Identify one unclear claim, one design risk, and one actionable revision. The team owns the shared proposal; each member contributes and discloses permitted AI assistance.

slides.title: Revisions and Their Reasons
lines: Resolve the highest-impact issue first.
Record what changed and why.
Preserve the original prediction for comparison later.
slides.notes: Allow quiet revision time. A useful revision log separates planned design changes from changes made after results are observed. The log later supports Project Part 2 and the reflection.

slides.title: From Draft to Week 3 Proposal
lines: Use this week to improve the team draft.
Submit the proposal at the end of Week 3.
Resolve pilot issues and freeze the plan in Week 4.
slides.notes: One team submission identifies every member and includes AI Attribution and contribution records. Exact dates are posted in Canvas. Full collection begins in Week 5 after the Week 4 freeze. This eight-week schedule supersedes the earlier four-week calendar; grading is governed by the confirmed assessment policy.

title: Handoffs, Recommendations, and Evidence
prework: Watch the Module 3 videos. Read the Meridian and Juno examples and complete the short interference notebook. Bring an idea for your individual Discussion 3.
output: An individual Discussion 3 draft and a proposed managerial outcome to discuss with your audit team.

slides.title: Handoffs, Recommendations, and Evidence
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M3S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: An Interface Suggests the Next Action
lines: An extra identity check changes the payment process.
What does the reviewer see before choosing?
slides.notes: Stripe’s public product page illustrates review suggestions and an option to start an authentication experiment. Adaptive 3DS refers to an additional identity check for a payment. The displayed revenue number is part of a company demonstration, not a measured result for our case. Ask students where a recommendation, risk assessment, or interim answer enters the decision process. Compare a direct decision with a decision after an explicit assessment while holding the underlying facts fixed. Manual review is described at https://docs.stripe.com/radar/transaction-reviews.

image.alt: The focused view of the official Stripe demo displays an Adaptive 3DS recommendation with a Start experiment control. 3DS adds customer authentication. Its revenue number is demo content.

slides.caption: Stripe public interface demonstration, captured November 2026.

slides.title: Meridian’s Illustrative Console Choice
lines: Conditional block rates: 0.63 and 0.41.
Fraud-judgment share: 9/11; assessed rate: 0.59.
Direct block rate: 0.69.
slides.notes: Meridian is fictional and these rates are illustrative. Ask students to calculate the weighted rate and identify what comparison is challenged by .69. Source: Nathan Yang, Case: The Intermediate Step; adapted to distinguish the fixed-rate benchmark from process-dependent alternatives.

chart.caption: Fictional Meridian example; imposed rates, not field estimates.

slides.title: The Meaning of the Difference
lines: Compute direct minus assessed.
State why 0.69 lies outside the fixed-rate bracket.
Name a process that could change conditional rates.
slides.notes: The difference is .10 and the bracket is [.41,.63]. The weighted identity holds within assessed records. Carrying its rates to the direct procedure is the additional assumption. Ask groups to propose an informative comparison rather than assert that every classical explanation has failed.

slides.title: Equal Block Rates, Different Errors
lines: Which outcomes matter beyond the block rate?
slides.notes: Both procedures block 40 of 100 attempts. A blocks 25 fraudulent and 15 legitimate payments; B blocks 10 fraudulent and 30 legitimate payments. Fraud not blocked is therefore 5 versus 20. These are imposed workshop counts with known ground truth, separate from Meridian’s decision rates. A block rate alone does not measure accuracy or welfare. Students specify a managerial outcome and the validation evidence needed for their own setting.

chart.caption: Imposed outcomes: 30 fraudulent and 70 legitimate attempts in each procedure.

slides.title: Listening and the Taste Profile
lines: A play can serve a temporary purpose.
What outcome would show that recommendations improved?
slides.notes: Spotify’s 2025 announcement documents a track-level exclusion control. The pictured distinction gives a real setting for Juno’s recommendation problem from the videos. Ask students to separate immediate playback, future recommendations, and the outcome the listener values. A temporary use does not by itself reveal a stable preference. Propose a comparison and a measure of recommendation quality; do not infer effectiveness or a quantum mechanism from the feature’s existence. Save the comparison for Discussion 3.

image.alt: Spotify’s official track menu shows Hide in this playlist separately from Exclude track from your taste profile. The latter is highlighted in the original image.

slides.caption: Spotify track-exclusion announcement, October 2025.

slides.title: What the Panel Represents
lines: Tier 1 checks the calculation using a simulator.
Tier 2 studies the model under documented prompts.
Tier 3 adds evidence from relevant people.
slides.notes: Have each group rewrite an overbroad sentence into a claim about the observed unit. A synthetic persona is not a human respondent. Bisbee et al., https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2024.5, provide a comparison between synthetic outputs and human survey evidence.

slides.title: The Assessment Draft
lines: Outline the handoff or recommendation issue for M3A1.
Name the outcome your project recommendation needs.
Bring the completed M3A2 run to the studio.
slides.notes: Give students individual writing time. The discussion brief specifies the post and peer response. The practice notebook is an ungraded checkpoint; it prepares the collection and analysis workflow.

prework: Watch Module 3 and complete the individual audit practice on supplied data. Bring the team proposal draft, six-condition battery, pilot plan, and contribution record.
output: A team proposal ready for the end of Week 3, with unresolved pilot questions assigned for Week 4.

slides.title: Research Proposal Clinic
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making

M3S2 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes: Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

slides.title: The Proposal and the Collection Plan
table: Pilot and freeze the collection plan
lines: What still needs a decision before submission?
slides.notes: The proposal is shared team work. Audit practice remains individual and ungraded. A pilot checks implementation; it is not the main collection. Do not present tentative grading weights as confirmed.
slides.caption: Approved eight-week sequence

slides.title: Match the Claim to a Comparison
table: AB versus BA under matched conditions
Direct F versus assessed A then F
lines: Name the outcome, denominator, and rival explanation.
slides.notes: Teams mark the exact question and population for each proposed claim. Use the established six-condition collection guide. A QQ result concerns aggregate paired-response probabilities and does not show that every person is internally consistent.
slides.caption: Proposal design exercise

slides.title: A Pilot Record That Can Be Replayed
table: A: yes, then B: no, then F: yes
lines: Can another team reconstruct this response path?
slides.notes: Use a small synthetic pilot or supplied demonstration. Retain actual responses in constructed conversations. Fresh-context arms use separate conversations. Preserve failed and retried calls with identifiers. Verify that a retry is not silently counted as a new respondent.
slides.caption: Fictional log entry; no API calls required in class

slides.title: Peer Review the Team Proposal
lines: Exchange the claim and design sections.
Identify one ambiguous choice and its consequence.
Write a concrete revision with a reason.
slides.notes: Review against the current team proposal rubric. Give each student an assigned review role. Check the company decision, sources, six conditions, model-panel scope, thresholds, analysis plan, and division of work. Avoid requesting new data just to make a result more favorable.

slides.title: Resolve the Highest Priority Issues
lines: Revise the shared proposal and contribution log.
slides.notes: This is a blank planning structure, not a prescribed division among particular people. Every member should understand the full design. Record what changed and why. Keep unresolved issues visible rather than silently filling them with assumed values.
slides.caption: Team working table

slides.title: Prepare the Week 3 Submission
lines: One proposal, with all team members identified.
Attach the battery, analysis plan, and attribution records.
Carry implementation checks into the Week 4 pilot.
slides.notes: The proposal is due at the end of Week 3; Canvas supplies the exact date. Main collection opens in Week 5. Finish with each member explaining one design choice and one condition that could change the interpretation.

title: Pilot Evidence and Interpretation
prework: Watch Module 4. Bring the submitted team proposal, a small pilot or supplied demonstration, and the interpretation rules. Main collection has not opened.
output: A pilot issue log, checked interpretation rules, and a prioritized repair list for the Week 4 freeze.

slides.title: Pilot Evidence and Interpretation
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M4S1 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes: Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

slides.title: A Pilot Checks the Procedure
lines: Which failure would stop full collection?
slides.notes: Distinguish the pilot’s implementation purpose from estimating a final substantive effect. Use supplied practice data if API access is unavailable. Collection begins in Week 5 after the freeze.
slides.caption: Pre-collection check

slides.title: Two Pilot Problems Can Look Similar
lines: What would you inspect before interpreting a difference?
slides.notes: Constructed teaching rates. Higher invalidity in B may reflect wording, formatting, or system behavior. Preserve all attempts and reasons for exclusions. Check whether failures depend on the response. Do not silently replace failures until the desired result appears.

chart.caption: Illustrative rates; the categories total 100% within each condition.

slides.title: A Verdict Needs a Condition
table: What practical claim is still unresolved?
lines: Add the assumption that makes each inference valid.
slides.notes: Teams apply their proposed thresholds. Nonrejection is not proof of absence. A small-effect conclusion requires the relevant interval to lie within the chosen practical tolerance. QQ alone does not select a unique mechanism.
slides.caption: Interpretation practice

slides.title: Troubleshoot the Pilot in Pairs
lines: Trace one record from prompt to result.
Separate a design issue from a coding issue.
Explain the proposed correction before applying it.
slides.notes: Use a peer team as reviewer. Check context retention, unique run IDs, response parsing, model version, and planned resampling unit. Keep changes and their rationale in the revision log. Avoid changing a substantive rule because a pilot estimate looks inconvenient.

slides.title: Record What Must Be Repaired
lines: Save a repair list with owners and evidence.
slides.notes: Teams fill their own rows. A repaired implementation must be rerun on a pilot. Store the reviewed proposal separately from the collection-ready protocol so changes are traceable. Do not delete prior versions from the project log.
slides.caption: Working example

slides.title: Prepare for the Freeze Meeting
lines: Bring the repaired protocol and a replayable pilot.
State any unresolved risk and its owner.
Keep the final conclusions open until collection.
slides.notes: The next live session freezes the collection plan. No team presentation or individual oral defense is due in Week 4 under the eight-week schedule.

title: Collection Plan Freeze
prework: Bring the repaired pilot, exact prompts, six-condition design, collector settings, analysis plan, thresholds, and contribution log.
output: A dated frozen collection plan, a replayable pilot, named responsibilities, and a deviation-log template.

slides.title: Collection Plan Freeze
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M4S2 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes: Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

slides.title: From Proposal to Collection
lines: Can the team run the same plan independently?
slides.notes: The freeze makes the planned procedure concrete before main outcomes are observed. Canvas provides the submission date and any instructor sign-off process. Do not invent a required new approval that is absent from the course instructions.
slides.caption: Week 4 checkpoint

slides.title: The Frozen Record
lines: Find one field that another person could interpret differently.
slides.notes: Use the existing collection guide. Freeze model version and settings where controllable; document version changes that the provider imposes. Retain access and cost constraints. Establish what happens when calls fail or budget limits are reached.
slides.caption: Team protocol checklist

slides.title: Test Exceptions before Collection
lines: Write the rule before a real exception occurs.
slides.notes: Run a small demonstration of one failure case. Preserve the original attempt and any retry. An exception rule must not condition on whether the result favors the hypothesis. Avoid collecting credentials in the shared document.
slides.caption: Fictional failure scenarios

slides.title: Exchange and Replay a Pilot
lines: Give another team a complete pilot record.
Ask them to reconstruct order and denominator.
Resolve disagreements in the written protocol.
slides.notes: A peer replay checks reproducibility rather than grading the team’s substantive conclusion. Confirm that peers can identify the intended unit of analysis and the context retained for each arm. Use supplied data if access is limited.

slides.title: Responsibilities and Deviations
lines: Set responsibilities without isolating knowledge in one member.
slides.notes: Each student remains responsible for understanding the audit for the individual defense. The deviation log records date, reason, affected records, and consequences. A necessary repair after the freeze remains visible and may narrow the claim.
slides.caption: Team working table

slides.title: Freeze the Plan and Open Collection Next Week
lines: Save the dated collection-ready version.
Collect in Weeks 5–6 under that version.
Keep new agency examples separate from the frozen study.
slides.notes: Week 5 opens the collection window. Week 6 closes it. Week 7 supports analysis and peer critique; Week 8 holds presentations and individual defenses. The new philosophy material can improve interpretation without adding unplanned experimental arms.

Students work individually for three minutes and compare in pairs. Introduce ontology, empirical evidence, epistemology, and normative inquiry in plain language. Categories can overlap. Ask how the claim would change if the skip option did not work.

slides.title: Three Procedures One Setting
lines: Propose a criterion; test it against all three cases.
slides.notes:
Use groups of three, each defending one case. A predictable deliberate response may express agency. Randomness alone supplies no purpose or control. Ask what record would distinguish requested delegation from an imposed reminder.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Free Will and a Choice-Theoretic Separation of Classical and Quantum Models, September 2026 revision; course philosophy primer. slides.title: Apply One Ranking across Direct Questions
lines: If off has the higher fixed value, which case satisfies A3?
slides.notes:
Teaching probabilities. Case A satisfies the binary standalone requirement with strict differences. Case B fails for the stated ranking. A change in a second answer alone is not the A3 comparison. Discuss what independent evidence would support the ranking.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Free Will and a Choice-Theoretic Separation of Classical and Quantum Models, September 2026 revision; course philosophy primer. slides.title: Evaluate a Definition of Agency
lines: State the concern your criterion addresses.
Give a case your criterion handles badly.
Revise the criterion and identify a measurement.
slides.notes:
Connect the exercise to conceptual engineering. A company may choose a convenient definition around existing controls. Require a reason for each criterion and evidence about effective operation, rather than counting visible buttons.

lines: Draft a paragraph that keeps these claims distinct.
slides.notes:
Use the frozen team study as the starting point. A synthetic-panel audit concerns the model tested. Do not change collection arms to make an agency claim. Identify any additional human or valuation evidence as future work. Each member explains one inferential step.

lines: Record the criterion and its purpose.
Retain the counterexample and the resulting revision.
Continue collection under the frozen plan.

slides.title: Compare the Same Target Question
lines: What is the difference, and which denominator is used?
slides.notes:
Fresh teaching values distinct from the lecture construction. Difference is 25 percentage points. The second bar includes all respondents reaching B, not only those giving a particular first answer. Before interpreting, specify comparable populations, wording, information, and uncertainty.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Free Will and a Choice-Theoretic Separation of Classical and Quantum Models, September 2026 revision; course philosophy primer. slides.title: Two Explanations for the Same Pattern
table: A stored state or response rule
lines: Propose an observation on which predictions could differ.
slides.notes:
Have one group describe a quantum account and another a memory account. Require a pre-specified prediction for a longer history or independent measure. A direct-versus-sequenced difference rejects a non-invasive fixed-response benchmark under the stated conditions, while state-changing classical processes remain possible.

table: Counts by persona and required arm
lines: Find one issue before more calls are made.
slides.notes:
Teams inspect current logs, without viewing results solely to choose favorable stopping. Keep exact model metadata and context rules. If access is blocked, use the supplied practice records and document the blocker. Do not store API keys in the project repository.

lines: Identify the affected records.
Apply the frozen exception rule.
Document any necessary deviation and its consequence.
slides.notes:
Use the agreed protocol, not a newly optimized response rule. Review duplicate IDs, malformed answers, and missing required arms. If a change affects comparability, retain separate labels and plan a sensitivity check.

Assign the remaining collection checks.

title: Reconsideration and Evidence

slides.title: Reconsideration and Evidence
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M6S1 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes:
Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

slides.title: Read the Histories
table: B alone and A then B
lines: Which histories must belong to the same respondent?
slides.notes:
Use the supplied practice data. For individual revision, first and return responses must be paired within one valid history. Across-condition rates can use comparable groups with appropriate uncertainty analysis. The worksheet uses constructed data and does not validate a psychological process.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: A is focus; B is connection

slides.title: The Same Totals Different Histories
lines: Calculate net change and individual revision.
slides.notes:
The supplied dataset has 100 complete histories. Initial and final off shares are 50%. Forty respondents switch, so net change is zero points and revision is 40%. This distribution is imposed for practice. No statistical or philosophical conclusion is drawn from it.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

slides.title: What Could Produce the Revision?
lines: Name a test that could challenge your preferred explanation.
slides.notes:
Compare with immediate repetition and with the record of intervening events. State the assumptions before applying projective-model bounds. Neither stable totals nor a high revision rate establishes agency.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: Interpretation exercise

slides.title: Close the Team Collection
lines: Check coverage against the frozen plan.
Retain valid, invalid, and failed attempt counts.
Record the model version and final collection date.
slides.notes:
Collection closes in Week 6. Use the protocol’s stopping rule. If an external issue prevents completion, document what is missing and its implications rather than silently adding a new design. Keep an immutable copy of the raw logs.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

slides.title: Prepare the Analysis Handoff
table: A reproducible table and run instructions
lines: Have a second member reproduce one denominator.
slides.notes:
Use the existing audit notebook. Check that paired-persona resampling follows the design. The new return-history exercise remains separate from the main audit unless it was already included in the frozen plan.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: Team analysis preparation

slides.title: Save the Closeout and Practice Results
lines: Record net change and revision with denominators.
Assign unresolved collection issues.
Bring reproducible results to the Week 7 studio.
slides.notes:
The supplied agency practice extends understanding of histories. It does not create a new graded assignment. Students can keep individual notes for the reflection while the team prepares its shared analysis.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

title: Authority and Consumer Interests
prework: Watch Module 6 L2 through the conclusion. Bring the team’s evidence table and a specific recommendation under consideration.
output: A recommendation paragraph that identifies the affected user, procedural authority, valuation assumptions, and a testable review condition.

slides.title: Authority and Consumer Interests
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M6S2 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes:
Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

slides.title: Follow the User’s Actual Path
lines: What observation would verify each claimed control?
slides.notes:
These are fictional interface paths, not screenshots of a real service. Students may draw the paths in their notes. Examine understanding, effort, accessibility, and the point at which the decision becomes binding. Equal final outcomes leave procedural authority unresolved.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: Fictional procedure comparison

slides.title: A Different Welfare Calculation
lines: What is the additional expected loss, and under which values?
slides.notes:
Practice values: renewal probabilities are 20% and 35%; declining is independently worth $10 more than renewing. Expected losses are $2 and $3.50; additional loss is $1.50. Hold the offer, values, and procedure costs fixed. If values are unknown, a monetary claim needs further evidence.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

chart.caption: Constructed practice example; baseline is always declining.

slides.title: Preserve Useful Delegation
lines: Redesign one path without assuming all reminders are harmful.
slides.notes:
Groups specify permission, refusal, and revision. Requested, informed, revocable delegation can support the user’s purpose. A redesign is a proposal; identify what user evidence would establish that it works.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: Design exercise

slides.title: Apply the Comparison to the Team Recommendation
lines: Name the person and goal affected.
Separate the response effect from the welfare claim.
State which authority the proposed change preserves.
slides.notes:
A synthetic-panel result supports a claim about model behavior under the tested protocol. Identify human or valuation evidence that would be needed before a broader conclusion. Keep the original company decision central.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

slides.title: Write a Review Condition
table: Values or offer no longer match
lines: Specify a measure, owner, and practical threshold.
slides.notes:
Use the team’s justified threshold rather than inventing one after seeing results. Make the review condition specific enough for a manager to act. Connect it to the report’s evidence table and the revision log.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.
slides.caption: Report development

slides.title: Prepare for Analysis and Peer Critique
lines: Save the recommendation and its assumptions.
List missing evidence as an explicit next step.
Bring the report draft and working figures to Week 7.
slides.notes:
Collection is closed. Week 7 is for troubleshooting, analysis, peer review, and drafting. Any further data collection requires a documented reason and must not be presented as part of the original frozen design.

Source basis: Nathan Yang, Agency and the Persistence of Choice, November 2026 draft; Agency Erosion, October 2026 draft; course philosophy primer. Practice data are constructed and are not observed human or model-panel results.

title: Audit Troubleshooting Studio
prework: Bring the frozen plan, closed collection, executed notebook, issue log, and draft evidence table. Revisit the relevant Module 2–4 videos as needed.
output: Reproducible analysis, resolved or documented blockers, and figures with clear denominators, intervals, and interpretation.

slides.title: Audit Troubleshooting Studio
lines: Quantum Approaches for Decision Making
Nathan Yang
M7S1 · 90-minute workshop
slides.notes: Students watch the relevant videos before this session. Use the deck for application and assessment progress. Timings are facilitation estimates; pause on each working slide for the activity.

slides.title: Choose the Issue That Blocks the Claim
table: Match the claim to the comparison
lines: Choose one issue and state its consequence.
slides.notes: Teams triage issues by their effect on validity, not by visual polish. The instructor circulates. If there is no blocker, audit a result another member produced.
slides.caption: Studio triage

slides.title: Reproduce One Result from Raw Records
lines: Can a teammate obtain the same number?
slides.notes: Use the approved notebook and protocol. Preserve provenance from raw records to a plotted result. Check that no retry is counted twice and that invalid cases follow the stated rule. Use a separate sensitivity analysis for necessary deviations.
slides.caption: Team reproducibility check

slides.title: A Small Estimate Can Remain Imprecise
lines: What additional display is needed before calling the effect small?
slides.notes: The chart intentionally supplies only two equal estimates. Students must add intervals on paper: narrow from 1 to 3 points; wide from −5 to 9. With a pre-specified ±4-point tolerance, only the narrow interval lies entirely inside. The missing intervals are the issue to identify. Values are constructed.

chart.caption: Incomplete teaching figure: intervals of 1 to 3 and −5 to 9 points.

slides.title: Repair the Figure and Its Explanation
lines: Show the comparison, denominator, and units.
Display uncertainty beside the estimate.
State the conclusion and the condition supporting it.
slides.notes: Teams revise a figure from their audit, not the teaching chart alone. Keep labels readable and avoid using color as the only distinction. Ask another team to explain the figure without the author’s narration. Check that the caption identifies model-panel evidence.

slides.title: Keep the Remaining Uncertainty Visible
lines: Assign an owner and a resolution or limitation.
slides.notes: A documented limitation can be the correct outcome. Avoid filling a missing comparison with an unsupported assumption. Record repairs, timing, and consequences in the revision log. Protect the original prediction from hindsight rewriting.
slides.caption: Example issues

slides.title: Prepare the Peer-Review Draft
lines: Save the executed analysis and final figure data.
Draft the claim, rival explanation, and recommendation.
Bring unresolved questions to the next session.
slides.notes: Week 7 Session 2 uses peer critique of the report and deck. The team should bring a coherent draft, even when its conclusion is inconclusive. Assessment rewards reasoning and evidence, not support for a favored model.

slides.title: Review the Claim and Its Support
lines: Write a precise question beside one unsupported sentence.

slides.title: Rehearse a Ten-Minute Client Story
lines: Decision and comparison.
Evidence, uncertainty, and a credible rival.
Recommendation and the condition for revision.

slides.title: Practice an Individual Defense
table: A rival test or new result
Evidence and reason for the change
lines: Each member answers without teammate prompting.
slides.notes: This rehearsal is formative. The assessed oral defense in Week 8 is individual, with no live AI assistance or teammate prompting. Each student must understand the entire audit, including parts produced by others.

slides.title: Turn Feedback into a Revision
lines: Preserve the original claim in the revision log.
slides.notes: Teams prioritize substantive repairs before appearance. Each student keeps private reflection notes about how evidence changed their reasoning. The reflection remains individual; it should not be jointly written.
slides.caption: Revision example

slides.title: Prepare the Final Week
lines: Confirm the team presentation and each defense slot.
Submit report, deck, logs, and individual reflection in Week 8.
Use Canvas for exact dates and confirmed assessment rules.
slides.notes: No new grade percentages are introduced by this deck. Check file accessibility and that links work without private credentials. The reflection follows the existing brief, including its stated length, unless the instructor posts a revision.

lines: Keep each response within its assigned time.
Individual speakers explain their own reasoning.
Observers record a question and a useful comparison.
